statement: 'Representation' is a noun and 'represent' is a verb.
explanation: The advert represents women. It is a positive representation.

statement: A close-up shows a person's whole body.
explanation: A close-up is very near: usually a face or a small detail.

statement: The foreground is the part of an image furthest away.
explanation: The foreground is at the front. The background is furthest away.

statement: A stereotype is a simple, fixed idea about a group.
explanation: For example, the idea that all teenagers are lazy.

statement: We say 'the advert is aimed at teenagers'.
explanation: A text is aimed at its target audience.

statement: 'Stereotypical' is an adjective.
explanation: a stereotypical image, a stereotypical role.

statement: 'Reinforce' means make an idea stronger.
explanation: It is the opposite of 'challenge'.

statement: To 'challenge' a stereotype means to agree with it.
explanation: Challenge = question it or go against it.

statement: Body language is what a person says.
explanation: It is how the body's position and movement show feelings.

statement: We say 'an effect on the audience'.
explanation: have an effect on someone.

statement: Costume is the clothing chosen for a character or model.
explanation: Costume is a creative choice that carries meaning.

statement: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase.
explanation: For example: 'Just do it'.

statement: 'The advert show a family' is correct.
explanation: 'The advert' is singular: the advert shows a family.

statement: 'Imply' means say something directly.
explanation: Imply = suggest an idea without saying it directly.

statement: The setting is where and when the image takes place.
explanation: For example, a modern office or a beach.

statement: 'Analyse' is the verb and 'analysis' is the noun.
explanation: We analyse the poster. My analysis focuses on colour.

statement: A headline is the title of a news story.
explanation: It is printed in large letters at the top.

statement: 'Vulnerable' means strong and safe.
explanation: Vulnerable = easily hurt and needing protection.

statement: 'Evidence' has a plural: 'evidences'.
explanation: Evidence is uncountable.

statement: 'An everyday kitchen' means a normal kitchen.
explanation: everyday (one word) = normal. every day (two words) = each day.

statement: The target audience is the group a text is made for.
explanation: For example, young women aged 18–25.

statement: 'The angle makes him looks powerful' is correct.
explanation: make someone + base verb: makes him look powerful.

statement: A camera is used to take photographs or film.
explanation: A camera records images.

statement: A camera is a type of clothing.
explanation: Clothing is worn; a camera records images.

statement: An image can be a photograph or a drawing.
explanation: Both photographs and drawings are images.

statement: An image must always be a photograph.
explanation: Drawings and digital pictures can also be images.

statement: Red, blue and green are colours.
explanation: These are all examples of colours.

statement: Colour means the words used in an advert.
explanation: The words are its language; colour means red, blue, green and so on.

statement: Clothing means clothes in general.
explanation: Shirts, coats and trousers are clothing.

statement: 'Clothing' normally has a plural: 'clothings'.
explanation: Clothing is uncountable; we do not normally say 'clothings'.

statement: A group is more than one person linked in some way.
explanation: A class or a football team can be a group.

statement: A group must contain only one person.
explanation: One person is an individual, not a group.

statement: 'Show' means make something clear or visible.
explanation: An image can show an idea or a person.

statement: 'Show' means hide something from the audience.
explanation: To hide is to keep something unseen; show means make it visible.

statement: The audience is the people who see, read or hear a media text.
explanation: Viewers, readers and listeners can all be audiences.

statement: The audience is the person who makes the advert.
explanation: The maker is the producer; the audience receives the text.

statement: The background is behind the main subject.
explanation: It is the part farther back in an image.

statement: The background is always at the front of an image.
explanation: The foreground is at the front; the background is behind.

statement: The foreground is the front part of an image.
explanation: Objects in the foreground appear nearest to us.

statement: The foreground is the part furthest from the audience.
explanation: The background is usually furthest away.

statement: A close-up often shows a face or one small detail.
explanation: A close-up brings the camera near the subject.

statement: A close-up always shows a person's whole body.
explanation: A whole-body view is not normally a close-up.

statement: The setting is where and when a scene happens.
explanation: A beach at sunset can be a setting.

statement: The setting means the colours used in a logo.
explanation: Colours are a design choice; the setting is the place and time.

statement: A costume is clothing chosen for a character or model.
explanation: Costume can help show a role or identity.

statement: A costume is the position of the camera.
explanation: That is the camera angle.

statement: A pose is the way somebody stands or sits for an image.
explanation: Hands on hips can be part of a pose.

statement: A pose is the title of a newspaper story.
explanation: The title is the headline.

statement: A facial expression is the look on a person's face.
explanation: A smile or frown is a facial expression.

statement: A facial expression is shown only by the feet.
explanation: It is shown on the face.

statement: Body language uses posture and movement to show feelings.
explanation: Crossed arms can be part of body language.

statement: Body language means the dialogue spoken by a character.
explanation: Dialogue uses words; body language uses the body.

statement: A slogan is a short phrase designed to be remembered.
explanation: Adverts often repeat slogans.

statement: A slogan is always a long paragraph.
explanation: Slogans are usually short and memorable.

statement: A news headline tells the audience what a story is about.
explanation: It is the story title, often printed in large letters.

statement: A headline is the music behind a video.
explanation: Music is sound; a headline is written language.

statement: Lighting is the way light is used in an image or scene.
explanation: Lighting can be bright, dark, soft or harsh.

statement: Lighting means the clothes worn by a model.
explanation: Those clothes are clothing or costume.

statement: 'Friendly' means kind and pleasant to other people.
explanation: A warm smile can make someone look friendly.

statement: 'Friendly' means angry and dangerous.
explanation: Angry and dangerous do not mean friendly.

statement: 'Caring' describes someone who wants to help others.
explanation: A caring character may comfort another person.

statement: 'Caring' means refusing to notice other people's needs.
explanation: Ignoring people is not caring behaviour.

statement: 'Serious' can describe someone who is not smiling or joking.
explanation: A serious expression may suit an important scene.

statement: 'Serious' always means very funny.
explanation: Funny and serious have different meanings.

statement: 'Strong' can mean physically powerful.
explanation: A weightlifter may be represented as strong.

statement: 'Strong' means unable to lift anything.
explanation: That would suggest weakness.

statement: 'Weak' means not strong.
explanation: A weak character may appear easy to defeat.

statement: 'Weak' and 'powerful' always mean the same thing.
explanation: Weak and powerful have different meanings.

statement: 'Modern' means new and up to date.
explanation: A glass office with new technology can look modern.

statement: 'Modern' means very old-fashioned.
explanation: Old-fashioned is the opposite of modern.

statement: Representation is how a person, group or idea is shown.
explanation: Media texts create representations through choices.

statement: Representation means hiding every person from the audience.
explanation: Representation concerns how something is shown.

statement: A wide smile can make a character look friendly.
explanation: The smile gives the audience a clear positive clue.

statement: A wide smile always proves that a character is angry.
explanation: A smile more commonly suggests happiness or friendliness.

statement: A dark background can make an image feel serious.
explanation: Darkness can help create a serious mood.

statement: A dark background must make every image cheerful.
explanation: Darkness does not automatically create a cheerful mood.

statement: A gold watch can suggest that a character is wealthy.
explanation: Gold and costly objects can communicate wealth.

statement: A gold watch shows that the character has no money.
explanation: The object is more likely to suggest wealth than poverty.

statement: A person in a white coat may be shown as a doctor.
explanation: Costume can help the audience recognise a role.

statement: A white coat is a type of camera angle.
explanation: It is clothing, not a camera position.

statement: A football shirt can show that someone supports a team.
explanation: Clothing can communicate group identity.

statement: A football shirt can never communicate identity.
explanation: It can show connection to a club or group.

statement: A close-up can help us see a character’s emotion.
explanation: It makes the face and expression easier to see.

statement: A close-up hides every detail of the face.
explanation: A close-up usually reveals facial detail.

statement: Bright lighting can make a cereal advert feel cheerful.
explanation: Bright light often supports a positive mood.

statement: Bright lighting always makes a cereal advert frightening.
explanation: Bright light does not automatically create fear.

statement: A low camera angle looks upward at a subject.
explanation: The camera is positioned below the subject.

statement: A low camera angle looks down from above.
explanation: Looking down from above is a high angle.

statement: A tidy suit can make a character look professional.
explanation: Smart costume can suggest skill and status.

statement: A tidy suit must make a character look like a baby.
explanation: The clothing does not give that meaning.

statement: A beach can be the setting of a holiday advert.
explanation: The beach is the place where the advert happens.

statement: A beach is a facial expression.
explanation: A beach is a place, so it is part of the setting.

statement: The words “Join us today” can be a slogan.
explanation: They form a short, memorable call to action.

statement: A slogan cannot contain words.
explanation: A slogan is made from words.

statement: A newspaper story can have a headline.
explanation: The headline names or introduces the story.

statement: A newspaper headline is always hidden under the page.
explanation: A headline is normally made easy to notice.

statement: Crossed arms are part of body language.
explanation: The position of the arms can communicate a feeling.

statement: Crossed arms are a colour palette.
explanation: They are a body position, not a set of colours.

statement: A frown is a facial expression.
explanation: It changes the appearance of the face.

statement: A frown is a type of setting.
explanation: It is an expression, not a place or time.

statement: A superhero standing tall has a powerful pose.
explanation: Standing tall can communicate confidence and strength.

statement: A superhero’s pose is the same thing as the background.
explanation: The pose belongs to the person; the background is behind them.

statement: A family can be shown as a happy group.
explanation: Several people may be represented together as a group.

statement: A family of four is one individual.
explanation: Four people form a group.

statement: An advert can use positive language such as “brilliant”.
explanation: The word praises the product.

statement: The word “brilliant” is negative language in every advert.
explanation: It is normally positive praise.

statement: An empty street can make a person look alone.
explanation: The setting can shape how the person is represented.

statement: An empty street must make the person look crowded.
explanation: An empty place cannot itself look crowded.

statement: A tiny mouse beside a huge cat may look weak.
explanation: The size contrast can make the mouse seem less powerful.

statement: A tiny mouse beside a huge cat must look stronger than the cat.
explanation: Its smaller size is more likely to suggest weakness.

statement: A crown can show that a character is a king or queen.
explanation: A prop can communicate a social role.

statement: A crown is always evidence that the character is a firefighter.
explanation: A crown normally suggests royalty.

statement: A robot in a shiny city may look modern.
explanation: The subject and setting both support a modern image.

statement: A shiny robot city must look ancient.
explanation: Robots and new technology usually suggest modernity.

statement: A nurse helping a patient can be represented as caring.
explanation: The action gives evidence of care.

statement: Helping a patient proves the nurse is careless.
explanation: Helping is evidence of caring behaviour.

statement: A character looking into the camera can connect with the audience.
explanation: Direct eye contact can feel personal.

statement: Looking into the camera makes the audience unable to see the character.
explanation: The character remains visible and may feel more direct.

statement: A red cape is part of a superhero’s costume.
explanation: The cape is clothing chosen for the character.

statement: A red cape is the setting of the scene.
explanation: It is worn by the character, so it is costume.

statement: A busy office in the background can show where someone works.
explanation: Background details can communicate the setting.

statement: Background details never add meaning to an image.
explanation: They can show place, time and context.

statement: To describe is to say what you can see or what something is like.
explanation: Description identifies visible or audible details.

statement: To describe is to explain every hidden reason behind a choice.
explanation: Explaining reasons goes beyond description.

statement: To explain is to say how or why something creates meaning.
explanation: An explanation connects a choice to an effect or idea.

statement: To explain is only to list objects in an image.
explanation: Listing objects is description, not explanation.

statement: A detail is a small part that you notice.
explanation: A ring, shadow or word can be a detail.

statement: A detail must be the whole media text.
explanation: A detail is one small part of the whole.

statement: Meaning is the idea or message communicated by a choice.
explanation: Colour, language and pose can all carry meaning.

statement: Meaning is only the price paid to make an advert.
explanation: Production cost is different from meaning.

statement: A creative choice is a decision made by the producer.
explanation: Choosing red lighting is a creative choice.

statement: A creative choice happens without anyone deciding anything.
explanation: A choice involves a decision.

statement: A reason explains why something happens or is done.
explanation: We can give a reason for using a close-up.

statement: A reason is always a visible object in the foreground.
explanation: An object can be evidence; a reason explains why.

statement: 'Ordinary' means normal and not special.
explanation: An ordinary kitchen may look like one used every day.

statement: 'Ordinary' means magical and impossible.
explanation: Magical and impossible are not ordinary.

statement: 'Everyday' as one word can mean normal or usual.
explanation: An everyday scene shows familiar daily life.

statement: 'Everyday' always means once a year.
explanation: Every day means each day; neither form means once a year.

statement: 'Confident' means sure of yourself and your abilities.
explanation: Open posture and eye contact may suggest confidence.

statement: 'Confident' means certain that you will fail.
explanation: That would suggest doubt, not confidence.

statement: 'Powerful' can mean having control or influence.
explanation: A leader may be represented as powerful.

statement: 'Powerful' means having no influence at all.
explanation: Having no influence is the opposite of being powerful.

statement: 'Successful' describes someone who has achieved an aim.
explanation: A trophy can help represent an athlete as successful.

statement: 'Successful' means never achieving anything.
explanation: That is the opposite meaning.

statement: 'Attractive' means pleasant or appealing to look at.
explanation: Adverts often make products look attractive.

statement: 'Attractive' means impossible to notice.
explanation: Something attractive is designed to appeal to people.

statement: 'Wealthy' means having a lot of money.
explanation: A mansion and luxury car may suggest wealth.

statement: 'Wealthy' means having no money.
explanation: That describes poverty, not wealth.

statement: A positive representation shows someone in a favourable way.
explanation: Words such as brave and caring create positive representations.

statement: A positive representation always attacks the person shown.
explanation: An attack would usually create a negative representation.

statement: A negative representation shows someone in an unfavourable way.
explanation: Calling a group lazy creates a negative view.

statement: A negative representation can only praise a group.
explanation: Praise normally creates a positive view.

statement: A realistic representation seems close to real life.
explanation: Mess, tired faces and ordinary clothes may add realism.

statement: A realistic representation must include magic powers.
explanation: Magic powers generally make a scene less realistic.

statement: A role is the position or job a person has in a situation.
explanation: Parent, leader and student are examples of roles.

statement: A role is always a camera movement.
explanation: A role describes a person’s position or function.

statement: Identity concerns who a person is and the groups they belong to.
explanation: Age, culture, interests and occupation may shape identity.

statement: Identity means only the colour of the background.
explanation: Background colour may communicate identity, but it is not identity itself.

statement: Stereotypes simplify groups into fixed, familiar ideas.
explanation: They ignore many differences between individuals.

statement: A stereotype is a detailed picture of every individual difference.
explanation: Stereotypes simplify groups instead of showing individual differences.

statement: The target audience is the particular group a text is made for.
explanation: A game advert may target teenagers.

statement: The target audience is always every person in the world.
explanation: Most texts are designed with a more specific group in mind.

statement: A producer creates or controls a media text.
explanation: A photographer, editor or advertiser can be a producer.

statement: The producer is simply anyone who sees the finished text.
explanation: People who receive the text form the audience.

statement: A prop is an object used in a scene or image.
explanation: A laptop or football can be a meaningful prop.

statement: A prop is the emotion shown on a face.
explanation: That is a facial expression.

statement: Composition is the arrangement of elements in an image.
explanation: Where people and objects are placed affects composition.

statement: Composition means only the volume of the music.
explanation: Volume is a sound choice, not visual composition.

statement: A symbol is something that stands for a wider idea.
explanation: A broken chain can symbolise freedom.

statement: A symbol can never communicate an idea.
explanation: Communicating another idea is what makes it symbolic.

statement: Contrast is a clear difference between two things.
explanation: Bright white against black creates visual contrast.

statement: Contrast means that two things are exactly the same.
explanation: Contrast depends on difference.

statement: A messy bedroom may make a teenage character seem realistic.
explanation: The familiar imperfection can resemble everyday life.

statement: A messy bedroom automatically represents every teenager as wealthy.
explanation: Mess does not by itself communicate wealth.

statement: A low angle can make a small dog look powerful.
explanation: Looking upward can increase the subject’s apparent status.

statement: A low angle always makes the subject look smaller and weaker.
explanation: A low angle often has the opposite effect.

statement: Soft lighting can make a family scene feel warm and safe.
explanation: The gentle light supports a comforting mood.

statement: Soft lighting can only create a violent mood.
explanation: Its effect depends on context, but it does not only create violence.

statement: The slogan “Made for adventure” suggests an active lifestyle.
explanation: The word adventure carries ideas of excitement and travel.

statement: The slogan “Made for adventure” presents the product as boring and inactive.
explanation: Its language suggests action and excitement.

statement: An empty chair beside a child may suggest loneliness.
explanation: The missing companion is a visual clue.

statement: An empty chair must represent the child as popular.
explanation: The clue is more likely to suggest absence or loneliness.

statement: A chef’s hat helps identify the character’s role.
explanation: The costume gives information about the job.

statement: A chef’s hat is evidence that the character is an astronaut.
explanation: It conventionally suggests a chef.

statement: A trophy can represent success.
explanation: It is evidence of winning or achievement.

statement: A trophy normally represents failure.
explanation: It more commonly symbolises achievement.

statement: A cracked phone can make an advert’s situation feel ordinary.
explanation: The imperfection can resemble everyday experience.

statement: A cracked phone must make the scene look perfect and luxurious.
explanation: Damage is more likely to reduce that sense of perfection.

statement: Calling a grandmother “fearless” creates a positive representation.
explanation: The adjective praises her courage.

statement: Calling a grandmother “useless” creates a positive representation.
explanation: The adjective is insulting and negative.

statement: A school poster showing many cultures can represent the school as diverse.
explanation: The range of people supports the idea of diversity.

statement: Showing many cultures proves that the school has only one kind of student.
explanation: The visible variety suggests the opposite.

statement: A character who repairs the spaceship alone may seem independent.
explanation: The action shows that the character can work without help.

statement: Working alone successfully always makes a character look dependent.
explanation: Successful solo action suggests independence.

statement: A father cooking dinner can challenge an old-fashioned family role.
explanation: It goes against the stereotype that cooking is only women’s work.

statement: A father cooking dinner always reinforces the idea that only women cook.
explanation: The image shows a man doing the cooking.

statement: A teenager helping a lost child can be represented as responsible.
explanation: The action gives clear evidence of sensible behaviour.

statement: Helping a lost child represents the teenager as careless.
explanation: The action suggests care and responsibility.

statement: The words “limited edition” can make a product seem special.
explanation: The phrase suggests rarity.

statement: “Limited edition” means the product is ordinary and unlimited.
explanation: The phrase says that only a limited number are available.

statement: A bright red button can attract the audience’s attention.
explanation: Strong colour contrast makes it easy to notice.

statement: A bright red button is designed to disappear into every background.
explanation: Bright contrast usually increases visibility.

statement: A close-up of trembling hands can communicate fear.
explanation: The detail gives evidence of nervousness.

statement: Trembling hands are always evidence of complete calm.
explanation: Trembling commonly suggests fear or anxiety.

statement: A crowded train can make a city seem busy.
explanation: The number of people supports the representation.

statement: A crowded train represents the city as empty.
explanation: Crowding communicates that many people are present.

statement: An eye-level camera angle can make a person seem equal to the viewer.
explanation: The camera does not obviously look up or down at them.

statement: An eye-level angle always makes the viewer look down on the person.
explanation: That effect belongs to a high camera angle.

statement: A tiny figure in a huge landscape may look vulnerable.
explanation: The scale makes the person seem exposed and less powerful.

statement: A tiny figure in a huge landscape must look dominant.
explanation: The composition is more likely to reduce the person’s power.

statement: A news photo can select one moment from a much longer event.
explanation: The chosen moment shapes what the audience sees.

statement: A single news photo shows every moment of an event.
explanation: One photograph cannot contain the whole event.

statement: Positive music can make a charity video feel hopeful.
explanation: Sound can guide the audience’s emotional response.

statement: Music has no effect on representation.
explanation: Sound choices can change mood and meaning.

statement: A luxury car beside a glass tower can suggest wealth and success.
explanation: Both the prop and setting carry status meanings.

statement: A luxury car and glass tower clearly suggest poverty.
explanation: These are conventional signs of wealth.

statement: A character hiding behind another person may seem less confident.
explanation: The position suggests uncertainty or fear.

statement: Hiding behind someone is the clearest sign of leadership.
explanation: The action usually reduces the character’s apparent confidence.

statement: A caption can change how the audience understands a photograph.
explanation: Words can guide the meaning attached to an image.

statement: A caption can never affect the meaning of a photograph.
explanation: Language beside an image can strongly shape interpretation.

statement: If an advert shows only young models, older people are omitted.
explanation: Omitted means left out.

statement: If an advert shows only young models, every age group is included.
explanation: Older groups are missing from the selection.

statement: To compare means to examine similarities and differences.
explanation: A useful comparison considers both texts.

statement: To compare means to discuss only one text.
explanation: A comparison requires at least two things.

statement: To contrast means to focus on differences.
explanation: Contrast draws attention to how things are unlike.

statement: To contrast means to prove that two images are identical.
explanation: Contrast depends on difference.

statement: An effect is the result a choice has on the audience.
explanation: The verb is affect; the noun is effect.

statement: In 'the lighting has an effect', effect is a verb.
explanation: Here effect names a result, so it is a noun.

statement: Evidence is a detail that supports a point.
explanation: A quotation or visible feature can provide evidence.

statement: Evidence is a personal guess with no support in the text.
explanation: Evidence must come from the text or image.

statement: To support a point is to provide evidence for it.
explanation: Details help prove that an analytical claim is reasonable.

statement: To support a point is to change the subject completely.
explanation: Relevant evidence must connect to the point.

statement: A target audience is more specific than the general audience.
explanation: It is the group the producer especially wants to reach.

statement: Target audience means every person who happens to see a text.
explanation: That describes the actual audience, which may be broader.

statement: A traditional role follows ideas that have existed for a long time.
explanation: A media text can repeat or challenge such a role.

statement: A traditional role must be new and unexpected.
explanation: Traditional ideas are established over time.

statement: A realistic image can still be carefully constructed.
explanation: Natural-looking lighting and poses may be planned choices.

statement: If an image looks realistic, no creative decisions were made.
explanation: Realism can itself be deliberately created.

statement: An independent character is shown as able to act without help.
explanation: Solo decisions and actions can communicate independence.

statement: An independent character must be controlled by everybody else.
explanation: That would represent dependence.

statement: A responsible character is presented as sensible and trustworthy.
explanation: Looking after others can provide evidence of responsibility.

statement: A responsible character cannot be trusted with anything.
explanation: Trustworthiness is part of responsibility.

statement: Professional clothing can suggest skill and status.
explanation: A uniform or suit may communicate a work identity.

statement: Professional clothing always makes a character look unemployed.
explanation: The clothing usually suggests a work role.

statement: We say 'represent someone as powerful'.
explanation: Represent is commonly followed by someone as an adjective or noun.

statement: We say 'represent someone of powerful'.
explanation: The correct pattern is 'represent someone as powerful'.

statement: Connotation is an idea or feeling associated with a sign.
explanation: Red may connote danger, love or energy depending on context.

statement: A connotation is only the dictionary definition of a word.
explanation: The direct dictionary meaning is denotation.

statement: Selection means choosing which details to include.
explanation: Every frame includes some possibilities and excludes others.

statement: Selection means showing everything that exists.
explanation: Media producers must choose what enters the frame.

statement: Omission means leaving something out.
explanation: What is absent can affect a representation.

statement: Omission means placing an object in the centre.
explanation: Centre placement is composition; omission is absence.

statement: A media producer makes choices that shape representation.
explanation: Writers, editors and photographers all select material.

statement: Representation appears without any choices from producers.
explanation: Media texts are constructed through choices.

statement: Framing controls what the camera includes and excludes.
explanation: The edge of the frame limits the audience’s view.

statement: Framing guarantees that the audience sees everything nearby.
explanation: Anything outside the frame is omitted.

statement: Editing can change the order and length of shots.
explanation: This can alter pace and meaning.

statement: Editing can only change the colour of costumes.
explanation: Editing covers a much wider range of choices.

statement: Music can influence how a person or event is represented.
explanation: Triumphant music may present an entrance as heroic.

statement: Music cannot contribute to meaning because it has no pictures.
explanation: Sound also shapes mood and audience response.

statement: A voice-over can guide the audience’s opinion of an image.
explanation: Spoken commentary can frame what viewers see.

statement: A voice-over is silent text at the bottom of the screen.
explanation: A voice-over is spoken narration.

statement: Genre creates expectations about characters and events.
explanation: Audiences expect different things from horror and comedy.

statement: Genre has no relationship with audience expectations.
explanation: Familiar genre patterns guide expectations.

statement: A preferred meaning is the interpretation encouraged by the text.
explanation: Creative choices can guide the audience toward it.

statement: A preferred meaning is guaranteed to be accepted by every viewer.
explanation: Audiences can negotiate or oppose the intended meaning.

statement: An analytical point should be linked to evidence.
explanation: The evidence shows where the interpretation comes from.

statement: A strong analysis needs no reference to the media text.
explanation: Without evidence, the claim is difficult to prove.

statement: A positive representation can still be stereotypical.
explanation: A group may be praised through a simple fixed idea.

statement: Every positive representation is automatically complex and fair.
explanation: Positive treatment does not remove simplification.

statement: A stereotype can appear in comedy as well as drama.
explanation: Genre does not prevent stereotypical representation.

statement: Stereotypes exist only in serious news reports.
explanation: They can appear across media forms and genres.

statement: An individual may share traits with a group without representing everyone in it.
explanation: One person cannot show every member of a diverse group.

statement: One character can prove what every member of a group is like.
explanation: A single example cannot establish a universal truth.

statement: The same costume can carry different meanings in different contexts.
explanation: A black suit may suggest professionalism, mourning or secrecy.

statement: A costume always has one fixed meaning in every media text.
explanation: Context changes how signs are understood.

statement: A headline can frame a person before the article is read.
explanation: Its language supplies an early interpretation.

statement: Headlines never influence audience expectations.
explanation: They can strongly shape the first impression.

statement: Camera distance affects how much detail and context we see.
explanation: A close-up reveals detail while a long shot shows more setting.

statement: Camera distance never changes the information in a shot.
explanation: Different distances include different visual information.

statement: The background can provide evidence about wealth or lifestyle.
explanation: Homes, workplaces and objects create social context.

statement: Only the main person can carry meaning in an image.
explanation: Background details also contribute to representation.

statement: Repeated images can normalise an idea.
explanation: Frequent exposure can make a representation seem familiar.

statement: Repetition always makes an idea disappear from memory.
explanation: Repetition usually increases familiarity.

statement: An advert may sell an identity as well as a product.
explanation: It can invite the audience to imagine a lifestyle.

statement: Adverts can communicate only price and product size.
explanation: Many adverts attach products to identities and values.

statement: A high camera angle looks down on the subject.
explanation: This can reduce apparent power in some contexts.

statement: A high camera angle places the camera below the subject.
explanation: That describes a low angle.

statement: Direct address speaks to the audience as “you”.
explanation: It creates a personal connection with the reader or viewer.

statement: Direct address avoids referring to the audience.
explanation: The pronoun you addresses the audience directly.

statement: A rhetorical question is asked for effect rather than an actual reply.
explanation: Adverts use it to make audiences think.

statement: Every rhetorical question requires the audience to send an answer.
explanation: Its main purpose is persuasive or expressive.

statement: A binary opposition places two contrasting ideas against each other.
explanation: Hero and villain is a common example.

statement: A binary opposition presents two ideas as exactly the same.
explanation: It depends on a strong contrast.

statement: Context includes the circumstances surrounding a media text.
explanation: Time, place and culture can affect meaning.

statement: Context means only the font size used in a headline.
explanation: Font size is one design choice, not the whole context.

statement: 'The advert is aimed to teenagers' is correct English.
explanation: We say 'aimed at teenagers'.

statement: 'The image suggests that he is powerful' is grammatically correct.
explanation: Suggest can be followed by 'that' and a complete clause.

statement: 'The woman which is smiling' is the normal form for a person.
explanation: Use 'who' for a person: the woman who is smiling.

statement: 'These details supports my point' has correct subject–verb agreement.
explanation: Details is plural, so write: these details support my point.

statement: To identify a feature is to name or point it out.
explanation: Identification answers what the feature is.

statement: To identify a feature requires a full essay on its effects.
explanation: Naming the feature is enough to identify it.

statement: Purpose is the reason a media text was created.
explanation: Purposes may include informing, persuading or entertaining.

statement: Purpose means the accidental response of one viewer.
explanation: That is a response, not the producer’s purpose.

statement: Audience response is how viewers, readers or listeners react.
explanation: A response may be emotional, intellectual or behavioural.

statement: Audience response means only the producer’s private intention.
explanation: Intention belongs to the producer; response belongs to the audience.

statement: An individual is one person considered separately from a group.
explanation: Individual detail can complicate a group stereotype.

statement: An individual is a category containing millions of people.
explanation: That is a group, not one individual.

statement: 'Suggest' introduces an idea supported but not proved by a detail.
explanation: Analysts often use suggest to make a careful inference.

statement: 'Suggest' means prove beyond any possible doubt.
explanation: Suggestion is more cautious than proof.

statement: 'Present' can mean show someone in a particular way.
explanation: A report may present a politician as decisive.

statement: 'Present someone as' means remove them from the text.
explanation: The phrase concerns how they are shown.

statement: 'Communicate' means pass a message or feeling to an audience.
explanation: Images, words and sounds can all communicate.

statement: Only spoken language can communicate meaning.
explanation: Visual and audio choices also communicate.

statement: Camera angle is the position from which the camera looks.
explanation: High, low and eye-level are common angles.

statement: Camera angle means the length of the soundtrack.
explanation: That is a sound or editing choice.

statement: A close-up restricts the frame to a face or small detail.
explanation: This can emphasise emotion or significance.

statement: A close-up always provides the widest possible view of the setting.
explanation: A long or wide shot gives more setting.

statement: Setting includes the place and time of a media text.
explanation: Setting can establish social and historical context.

statement: Setting is another word for facial expression.
explanation: Expression belongs to the face; setting concerns place and time.

statement: A pose is a deliberately held body position.
explanation: It can communicate confidence, vulnerability or status.

statement: A pose is the natural light available in a location.
explanation: That relates to lighting.

statement: A facial expression communicates emotion through the face.
explanation: Eyes, eyebrows and mouth can all carry meaning.

statement: A facial expression can be read only from a person’s shoes.
explanation: It is visible on the face.

statement: Body language includes posture, gesture and movement.
explanation: It can support or contradict spoken words.

statement: Body language must always communicate exactly what dialogue says.
explanation: Bodies and words can send conflicting signals.

statement: Lighting controls the quality, direction and amount of light.
explanation: It can shape visibility, mood and status.

statement: Lighting affects brightness but can never affect mood.
explanation: Light is a major tool for creating mood.

statement: A slogan is a brief memorable phrase linked to a brand or campaign.
explanation: Its repetition can strengthen brand identity.

statement: A slogan is the same as a full terms-and-conditions document.
explanation: Slogans are concise and memorable.

statement: Framing is the selection of what appears within the image boundary.
explanation: It shapes both emphasis and omission.

statement: Framing includes every event outside the camera’s view.
explanation: Events outside the boundary are excluded.

statement: Denotation is the direct, literal meaning of a sign.
explanation: A denotation of a rose is that it is a flower.

statement: Denotation means all the emotional associations of a sign.
explanation: Those associations are connotations.

statement: Connotation is an associated idea or feeling.
explanation: A rose may connote romance in a particular context.

statement: Connotation is always identical in every culture and context.
explanation: Associations can vary between audiences and contexts.

statement: Selection is the process of choosing what to include.
explanation: Selection helps construct a version of reality.

statement: Selection gives the audience unfiltered access to everything.
explanation: Choosing material creates a limited version.

statement: Omission is the exclusion of information or people.
explanation: Omission can make a representation incomplete.

statement: Omission means adding every available viewpoint.
explanation: It means leaving something out.

statement: Juxtaposition places elements beside each other to create a comparison.
explanation: The relationship between the elements produces meaning.

statement: Juxtaposition requires the two elements never to appear near each other.
explanation: They must be placed together or closely connected.

statement: Anchorage uses words to guide the meaning of an image.
explanation: A caption can anchor an otherwise ambiguous photograph.

statement: Anchorage removes all language from a media text.
explanation: It uses language to narrow interpretation.

statement: A preferred reading is the interpretation encouraged by the producer.
explanation: Codes and conventions can direct audiences toward it.

statement: A preferred reading is the only interpretation audiences are physically able to make.
explanation: Audiences may negotiate or reject it.

statement: Bias is a tendency to favour one perspective over another.
explanation: Selection and language can reveal bias.

statement: Bias guarantees that every statement in a text is factually false.
explanation: A biased text may still contain accurate facts.

statement: A counter-stereotype deliberately reverses an expected representation.
explanation: It can challenge familiar assumptions.

statement: A counter-stereotype simply repeats the expected role unchanged.
explanation: Its defining feature is reversal or opposition.

statement: Placing a laughing child beside a ruined building creates juxtaposition.
explanation: The contrast may emphasise innocence, resilience or inequality.

statement: Placing two contrasting images together removes any possibility of comparison.
explanation: Juxtaposition invites comparison between them.

statement: The caption “Troublemakers return” anchors a crowd photograph negatively.
explanation: The noun guides viewers to interpret the crowd as threatening.

statement: A negative caption cannot influence the meaning of a neutral photograph.
explanation: Language can frame an image before it is examined closely.

statement: Showing only the winning moment selects one part of the athlete’s story.
explanation: Training, failure and uncertainty are omitted.

statement: One victory photograph provides a complete record of the athlete’s life.
explanation: It represents only a selected moment.

statement: A perfume advert can associate its product with independence.
explanation: The represented lifestyle may be part of what the advert sells.

statement: Product adverts can never sell values or identities.
explanation: Advertising frequently links products with desired identities.

statement: A hero filmed from below and centred in the frame is given visual authority.
explanation: Angle and composition combine to increase status.

statement: Filming a hero from below necessarily makes the hero invisible.
explanation: The angle changes apparent power, not basic visibility.

statement: If every scientist shown is male, the pattern may reinforce a gender stereotype.
explanation: Repeated exclusion can imply that science belongs to men.

statement: Showing only male scientists automatically challenges gender stereotypes.
explanation: The narrow selection repeats a familiar imbalance.

statement: A comedy can use a stereotype while also inviting the audience to laugh at it.
explanation: Tone and context affect whether a stereotype is reinforced or questioned.

statement: If a stereotype appears in comedy, it is automatically harmless.
explanation: Comedy does not remove possible effects or meanings.

statement: A character’s confident dialogue can be undermined by nervous body language.
explanation: The conflicting codes create a more complex representation.

statement: Body language must always confirm the words being spoken.
explanation: Visual behaviour can contradict dialogue.

statement: A charity advert may use a close-up to individualise a large social issue.
explanation: One face can make an abstract problem feel personal.

statement: A close-up always provides detailed statistics about the whole issue.
explanation: It personalises but does not supply complete statistical context.

statement: A negotiated reading accepts some of a text’s message but questions other parts.
explanation: The audience partly agrees while adapting the meaning.

statement: A negotiated reading means accepting every message without reservation.
explanation: That is closer to a preferred reading.

statement: An oppositional reading rejects the preferred meaning.
explanation: The audience interprets the text against its intended message.

statement: An oppositional reading is complete agreement with the producer.
explanation: It resists rather than accepts the encouraged interpretation.

statement: A news editor’s choice of photograph can alter a politician’s representation.
explanation: A smile and a grimace create different impressions.

statement: Photograph selection cannot affect a news story’s tone.
explanation: Images contribute strongly to tone and representation.

statement: Calling protesters a “mob” rather than a “crowd” adds a negative connotation.
explanation: The noun suggests disorder and threat.

statement: “Mob” and “crowd” carry exactly the same associations.
explanation: Mob is usually more negative and disorderly.

statement: A spotless home may construct an idealised family lifestyle.
explanation: The controlled setting removes everyday mess and difficulty.

statement: A spotless advertising set is always an unplanned record of ordinary life.
explanation: Such settings are commonly styled and selected.

statement: Representing one older character as adventurous can challenge expectations.
explanation: The individual is given traits often reserved for younger heroes.

statement: An adventurous older hero necessarily reinforces the idea that older people are inactive.
explanation: The representation contradicts that idea.

statement: A diverse cast does not by itself guarantee complex representation.
explanation: Characters may still be tokenistic or stereotyped.

statement: Including several social groups automatically makes every representation fair and detailed.
explanation: Quality depends on roles, depth and agency as well as presence.

statement: Giving a character agency means allowing them to make meaningful choices.
explanation: Agency affects how active or passive the representation seems.

statement: A character with agency can never influence the story.
explanation: Influencing events is central to agency.

statement: A product placed in the foreground receives visual emphasis.
explanation: Its proximity and scale can attract attention.

statement: Foreground placement is designed to make an object impossible to notice.
explanation: It usually makes the object more prominent.

statement: Harsh overhead lighting can produce an intimidating representation.
explanation: Deep shadows may make facial features appear severe.

statement: Lighting direction has no effect on the appearance of a face.
explanation: Direction changes highlights and shadows.

statement: The same red colour can connote romance in one text and danger in another.
explanation: Context changes the associations attached to a sign.

statement: Red has one universal meaning that never changes.
explanation: Colour meanings are shaped by context and culture.

statement: A headline phrased as a question can introduce doubt without making a direct accusation.
explanation: The grammar lets the text imply suspicion cautiously.

statement: A question headline can never influence the reader’s view.
explanation: Even without an answer, it can frame the subject.

statement: A documentary can be factual while still constructing a representation.
explanation: Filming, selection and editing shape the account.

statement: Factual media contain no framing or selection choices.
explanation: Facts are presented through chosen structures and images.

statement: If women speak for ten seconds and men speak for ten minutes, screen time creates an imbalance.
explanation: Quantity of voice can shape whose viewpoint seems important.

statement: Unequal speaking time cannot affect representation.
explanation: Prominence and voice are part of representation.

statement: A stereotype may help an audience recognise a character quickly.
explanation: Its familiarity can make communication efficient.

statement: Because stereotypes are quick to recognise, they can never cause harm.
explanation: Efficiency does not remove the risk of unfair simplification.

statement: A media text can challenge one stereotype while reinforcing another.
explanation: Representations may contain mixed or contradictory ideas.

statement: A text must be either completely progressive or completely stereotypical.
explanation: Different elements can work in different directions.

statement: To analyse is to explain how specific choices construct meaning.
explanation: Analysis connects evidence, method and effect.

statement: To analyse is merely to state whether you liked a text.
explanation: Personal preference alone is not analysis.

statement: Analysis is a detailed examination of how a text creates meaning.
explanation: It moves beyond feature spotting to relationships and effects.

statement: Analysis means copying the text without comment.
explanation: Copying provides material but no explanation.

statement: Representation is a constructed version of people, places or ideas.
explanation: Selection, framing and language shape that version.

statement: Representation is a perfectly neutral copy of reality.
explanation: Every media text selects and organises material.

statement: 'Represent' is a verb and 'representation' is a noun.
explanation: A film represents a group; the result is a representation.

statement: 'Represent' and 'representation' are both adjectives.
explanation: Represent is a verb and representation is a noun.

statement: A stereotypical representation reduces a group to familiar fixed traits.
explanation: It treats difference within the group as unimportant.

statement: A stereotypical representation always explores individual complexity.
explanation: Stereotypes simplify rather than deepen individuality.

statement: Identity can involve several overlapping social positions.
explanation: Age, gender, class, culture and profession may interact.

statement: Identity is determined by one feature only.
explanation: People have multiple and changing aspects of identity.

statement: A text implies; an audience infers.
explanation: Implication is encoded in the text, while inference is made by the receiver.

statement: An audience implies a hidden meaning placed there by the producer.
explanation: The audience normally infers; the text implies.

statement: To challenge a stereotype is to question or oppose it.
explanation: A counter-example can destabilise a familiar assumption.

statement: To challenge a stereotype is to repeat it without alteration.
explanation: Unchanged repetition is more likely to reinforce it.

statement: To reinforce a stereotype is to make it seem stronger or more familiar.
explanation: Repetition can naturalise the assumption.

statement: To reinforce a stereotype is to prove it has disappeared.
explanation: Reinforcement strengthens rather than removes it.

statement: 'Vulnerable' means open to harm or in need of protection.
explanation: Scale, isolation and posture can construct vulnerability.

statement: 'Vulnerable' means completely protected from all danger.
explanation: That is the opposite of vulnerable.

statement: The foreground is the area nearest the viewer within an image.
explanation: Foreground placement often grants visual prominence.

statement: The foreground is necessarily outside the frame.
explanation: It is a visible part at the front of the composition.

statement: Ideology is a connected set of beliefs about society and how it should work.
explanation: Media texts can reproduce or question ideological assumptions.

statement: Ideology means the technical resolution of an image.
explanation: Resolution concerns image quality, not social beliefs.

statement: Hegemony describes power maintained partly through accepted ideas and norms.
explanation: Dominant values may appear natural rather than imposed.

statement: Hegemony refers only to the brightness of a screen.
explanation: It concerns social and cultural power.

statement: Encoding is the producer’s construction of meaning through signs and codes.
explanation: Camera, language and editing choices can encode a preferred meaning.

statement: Encoding is the audience’s complete rejection of a message.
explanation: Audience interpretation is decoding.

statement: Decoding is the audience’s interpretation of encoded signs.
explanation: Different experiences can produce different readings.

statement: Decoding guarantees every audience member reaches the same meaning.
explanation: Interpretation can vary.

statement: A negotiated reading combines acceptance and resistance.
explanation: The audience accepts part of the preferred meaning but modifies it.

statement: A negotiated reading contains no engagement with the preferred meaning.
explanation: It partly accepts that meaning.

statement: An oppositional reading understands but rejects the preferred meaning.
explanation: The audience reads the text against its intended position.

statement: An oppositional reading fails to notice that the text communicates anything.
explanation: It recognises the preferred meaning before resisting it.

statement: Intersectionality examines how aspects of identity interact.
explanation: Gender, class and ethnicity may shape experience together.

statement: Intersectionality treats every identity category as completely separate.
explanation: It focuses on their interaction.

statement: Tokenism is superficial inclusion used to create an appearance of diversity.
explanation: A token character may be present but lack depth or agency.

statement: Tokenism guarantees detailed and equal representation.
explanation: Its inclusion is often limited or symbolic.

statement: Othering represents a group as fundamentally different from “us”.
explanation: The distinction can distance or dehumanise the group.

statement: Othering removes all boundaries between social groups.
explanation: It creates and emphasises a boundary.

statement: To marginalise is to push a person or group away from power or attention.
explanation: Limited voice and visibility can produce marginalisation.

statement: To marginalise is to place a viewpoint at the centre of public attention.
explanation: That would increase prominence rather than reduce it.

statement: Normalisation makes an idea appear ordinary or natural through repetition.
explanation: Repeated representations can reduce the sense that an idea is constructed.

statement: Normalisation always makes an idea seem strange and exceptional.
explanation: It makes the idea feel familiar.

statement: A counter-stereotype reverses or resists a familiar expectation.
explanation: It can broaden the roles associated with a group.

statement: A counter-stereotype is identical to the stereotype it challenges.
explanation: It departs from the familiar pattern.

statement: Polysemy means that a sign or text can support multiple meanings.
explanation: Context and audience knowledge affect which meaning is chosen.

statement: Polysemy means that a text permits exactly one interpretation.
explanation: The term refers to plurality of meaning.

statement: Agency is the capacity to act and influence events.
explanation: Characters with agency make consequential choices.

statement: Agency means existing only as a passive object for others.
explanation: Passivity indicates reduced agency.

statement: A seemingly empowering advert may still define success through beauty and consumption.
explanation: Its positive tone can coexist with a restrictive ideology.

statement: An empowering tone prevents an advert from carrying any limiting assumptions.
explanation: Different layers of meaning can contradict one another.

statement: A single heroic female character may challenge gender expectations without transforming the wider pattern.
explanation: One counter-example does not erase repeated marginalisation elsewhere.

statement: One counter-stereotype permanently removes the stereotype from culture.
explanation: Cultural patterns depend on many texts and institutions.

statement: When a refugee speaks for herself, the text grants more agency than when others speak about her.
explanation: Voice allows the represented person to frame her own experience.

statement: Removing a person’s voice necessarily increases that person’s agency.
explanation: It reduces control over the representation.

statement: A luxury advert can make wealth appear natural by excluding labour, debt and inequality.
explanation: Omission helps construct an effortless lifestyle.

statement: Omitted information cannot contribute to ideological meaning.
explanation: Absence can hide causes and alternatives.

statement: A documentary interview is constructed even when the speaker’s words are authentic.
explanation: Question choice, framing and editing shape the encounter.

statement: Authentic speech makes all production choices irrelevant.
explanation: Authenticity and construction can exist together.

statement: A stereotype may be recognised and criticised by one audience but accepted by another.
explanation: Decoding varies with experience, knowledge and social position.

statement: All audiences decode a stereotype in exactly the same way.
explanation: Audience readings are not mechanically identical.

statement: Repeated comic portrayals of incompetence can normalise a negative group image.
explanation: Humour does not prevent repetition from building familiarity.

statement: Comedy is outside representation and therefore cannot reinforce ideas.
explanation: Comic texts also construct social meanings.

statement: The phrase “people like us” can create belonging while also producing an excluded “them”.
explanation: Inclusive language can have an othering boundary.

statement: Inclusive pronouns can never imply exclusion.
explanation: The category us logically distinguishes those outside it.

statement: A high-status costume can encode authority before a character speaks.
explanation: Uniforms and formal clothing carry institutional connotations.

statement: Costume can communicate meaning only after dialogue explains it.
explanation: Visual codes can work immediately.

statement: A photograph’s apparent spontaneity can itself be a carefully designed effect.
explanation: Cropping, timing and pose may manufacture naturalness.

statement: A natural-looking image proves that no construction occurred.
explanation: Aesthetic realism can be planned.

statement: If a news report names one group’s ethnicity but not another’s, the uneven labelling may mark the first group as different.
explanation: Selective naming can contribute to othering.

statement: Unequal labels are always neutral and meaningless.
explanation: Patterns of naming can signal who is treated as the norm.

statement: A character can possess narrative agency while remaining morally flawed.
explanation: Agency concerns capacity to act, not goodness.

statement: Only morally admirable characters can have agency.
explanation: Villains and flawed characters may drive events.

statement: A negotiated reader may enjoy an advert’s humour while rejecting its gender politics.
explanation: Acceptance and resistance can occur at the same time.

statement: Partial agreement is impossible in audience interpretation.
explanation: Negotiated readings are defined by partial acceptance.

statement: Foregrounding one protester’s violence can marginalise the peaceful majority.
explanation: Selection may make an exceptional act represent the whole event.

statement: One selected act automatically provides a balanced account of every participant.
explanation: The frame may distort the proportions of the event.

statement: A diverse ensemble can still reproduce hierarchy if minority characters lack dialogue and decisions.
explanation: Visibility alone does not guarantee voice or agency.

statement: Equal presence in a poster guarantees equal narrative power.
explanation: Narrative importance also depends on action, speech and development.

statement: An oppositional reader can understand the intended patriotic message and still reject it.
explanation: Rejection does not require misunderstanding.

statement: Oppositional reading means being unable to identify the preferred message.
explanation: The reader may recognise it clearly.

statement: A stereotype can contain a flattering trait and still be restrictive.
explanation: Reducing a group to “naturally caring” limits individuality and roles.

statement: Positive adjectives make stereotyping impossible.
explanation: Simplification can be restrictive even when it sounds complimentary.

statement: When illness is represented only through tragedy, recovery and ordinary life are omitted.
explanation: The narrow pattern may define the identity through suffering.

statement: A tragic narrative necessarily represents the full range of experiences.
explanation: One narrative frame cannot provide that range.

statement: A media text may challenge dominant ideology through satire.
explanation: Exaggeration can expose contradictions in accepted beliefs.

statement: Satire always asks the audience to accept dominant ideas literally.
explanation: Satire often invites critical distance.

statement: Polysemy does not mean that every interpretation is equally supported.
explanation: Readings still need evidence from the text and context.

statement: If a text has several meanings, evidence becomes unnecessary.
explanation: Plausible readings must remain grounded in textual detail.

statement: A brand can appropriate the language of social change for commercial purposes.
explanation: Progressive language may be used to sell products and identity.

statement: Commercial purpose prevents a campaign from referring to social values.
explanation: Advertising often combines commercial and social messages.

statement: The absence of disabled characters can contribute to marginalisation even without an insulting stereotype.
explanation: Systematic invisibility limits who is imagined as part of ordinary life.

statement: Only openly negative images can marginalise a group.
explanation: Exclusion and silence can also marginalise.

statement: An image can encode vulnerability through scale while dialogue encodes confidence.
explanation: Conflicting codes can construct an ambivalent representation.

statement: Different media codes must always communicate one simple message.
explanation: Complex texts can contain tension and contradiction.

statement: Historical context can change the significance of a representation.
explanation: A role that once resisted convention may later appear familiar.

statement: Representations keep exactly the same cultural meaning forever.
explanation: Meanings shift as social norms and knowledge change.

statement: Critical analysis distinguishes the producer’s purpose from the text’s possible effects.
explanation: An intended joke may still reinforce a damaging assumption.

statement: A harmless intention guarantees a harmless audience effect.
explanation: Intention does not control every interpretation or consequence.
